Pachyuromys duprasi

The fat-tailed gerbil is a small rodent of the northern Sahara and the only species in its genus. It was first described in 1880 from Laghouat, in Algeria. It is listed as Least Concern and is best known for its short, swollen tail.

A round-bodied gerbil with a head and body of about 108 mm and a weight near 36 g. The long, fluffy fur is grey to tan, with a white belly and feet. The eyes are large and oval and the pink ears sit low on the head. The tail is shorter than the body, thick and club-shaped, without a tuft, and stores fat and water.

It lives in sand sheets with some vegetation, and sometimes in rocky desert. The Mammal Diversity Database gives its range as the northern Sahara from Western Sahara and Morocco to northern Egypt, while Animal Diversity Web describes it mainly west of the Nile Delta, into Libya, Tunisia and Algeria. It digs burrows up to about 1 m deep and sometimes uses those of other rodents.
In the wild it is mostly insectivorous, but it also eats plants, such as the desert shrubs Anabasis articulata and Artemisia monosperma.

It is mainly nocturnal, though often active at dusk, and spends much of its life in burrows. It is found in colonies but can also live alone. Males mark territory with scent glands on the belly. It is docile when handled and rarely bites, but can be aggressive toward others of its own species.

Gestation lasts 19–22 days and a litter holds 3–9 young, 4.5 on average; up to three litters a year are possible. Young are born blind and naked, are cared for by the female alone and are weaned at 3–4 weeks. Maturity comes at 3–6 months. Much of this information comes from captive animals and mostly from the Egyptian subspecies.

Its digging may aerate desert soil, and it probably affects local insect and plant populations. Birds are likely predators, but predation is poorly documented. The pale fur and the burrowing habit may help it avoid predators.
It is listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List. The sources read give no population estimate and no specific threat for wild animals.

Common Palm Civet
Paradoxurus hermaphroditus

The common palm civet is a nocturnal, tree-dwelling carnivoran of the civet family that lives in the forests of southern and south-eastern Asia and has adapted well to gardens, plantations and villages. It eats mostly fruit despite belonging to the order Carnivora.

A slender civet weighing about 1.3 to 5 kg, with a head and body of roughly 43–71 cm and a tail almost as long as the body, tipped with black but without rings. The coat is short and coarse, grey to blackish, with black-tipped guard hairs, dark stripes down the back and rows of black spots along the flanks. White patches on the face give it a masked look.

It lives in tropical and temperate forests and also in parks, suburban gardens, orchards and plantations, preferring tall trees with dense canopy and vines. It rests by day in tree hollows, rock crevices or thick foliage, and is recorded from sea level to about 2,000 m.

It is an opportunistic omnivore that leans heavily on fruit. In a secondary forest in West Java, fruit and seeds occurred in almost all droppings (97.6 %), animal remains in about a fifth. In an Indian sanctuary in winter, insects were the most frequent item in droppings, followed by fig fruit, birds and rodents.

Mostly solitary and active at night, it climbs trees to feed and rests in them by day. It stalks and pounces on animal prey. It is generally silent, snarling or hissing when alarmed, and marks surfaces with scent from a gland near the base of the tail.

Breeding can occur year-round, with up to two litters a year. After a gestation of about two months, a litter of two to five young is born, often in a tree hollow or rock crevice. Eyes open at about 11 days, young are weaned around two months and independent at about three months, according to a university database.

By eating fruit and passing seeds, it acts as a seed disperser: seeds of at least eight plant species were found in its droppings in West Java, and palm seeds are deposited far from the parent tree. It also eats rodents, and is preyed on by large cats, big snakes and crocodiles.

The Mammal Diversity Database lists it as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List. Animal Diversity Web reports legal protection in India and some other regions and names logging and forest clearing for oil palm plantations as threats. Taxonomy is under revision: the database now treats the species in a narrower sense than before, so older figures may cover several species.

The marbled cat is a small forest cat of South and South-East Asia, about the size of a house cat, with a long tail and a coat marked like that of a clouded leopard. It is rarely seen and poorly studied, and is listed as Near Threatened.

A cat with a body of 45–61 cm, a tail of 35–55 cm and a weight of 2.4–5 kg. The coat is yellowish brown with large blotches, paler in the centre and outlined in black, and black lines on the head, neck and back. The tail is spotted, black at the tip and usually held horizontally when walking. The ears are short and rounded, the feet large and the canines big for its size. Young are mottled brown until about four months.

It depends on forest and has not been found inside oil palm plantations. It is recorded in mixed deciduous-evergreen forest, secondary and logged forest, from sea level to about 3,000 m. Its range runs from the eastern Himalayan foothills through mainland South-East Asia to Sumatra and Borneo; its presence in Bangladesh and Bhutan is uncertain.

Its diet is poorly known. Birds, up to the size of a pheasant, are thought to be the main prey, along with tree squirrels, tree shrews, rodents, small primates, fruit bats, lizards, frogs and insects. This rests on few observations, such as a cat seen stalking birds in the canopy.

It is solitary and a skilled climber, able to come down tree trunks head first, but it is not limited to trees and also walks on the ground. It was long thought to be nocturnal, yet camera traps and sightings show activity by day as well as by night. One radio-collared female in Thailand used a range of about 5.3 km², a single animal that cannot stand for the species.

Nearly everything known comes from captivity: gestation of 66–82 days and litters of 2–4 kittens, usually two. Eyes open at about 16 days, kittens walk at about 22 days, eat solid food around 59 days and females mature at 21–22 months. The female raises the young alone. Breeding has not been documented in the wild.

It is a predator of birds and small mammals. No predator of the marbled cat is documented. In three Sabah study areas in Borneo, camera traps gave densities of 7.1 (upland primary forest), 10.5 (logged lowland forest) and 19.6 (lowland primary forest) animals per 100 km²; the authors suggest these may be at the high end of the species’ abundance.

It is listed as Near Threatened since 2015, having been Vulnerable in 2008; this change does not mean its numbers have risen or its threats lessened, as the species is still poorly studied. Forest loss is the main threat, and indiscriminate snaring is probably a major one. It is in CITES Appendix I.

The Eurasian tree sparrow is a small, sociable sparrow of farmland edges. In Britain it has suffered a severe long-term decline, and it is a Red-listed species there despite a recent small recovery from a very low level.

Slightly smaller than a house sparrow, an adult weighs about 21 g and has a wing length near 70 mm. It has a chestnut crown and nape, white cheeks with a black spot, a small black bib and a streaky brown back. Males and females look alike, and juveniles resemble faded adults.

In Britain and Ireland it lives mainly in eastern and lowland areas and is most frequent on arable farmland in the breeding season. In winter it gathers in flocks on stubble fields and sometimes visits garden feeders in rural villages.

It eats seeds of grasses and weeds and cultivated grain such as barley and wheat, and catches small insects to feed its young. Chicks fed more seed and fewer invertebrates fledged less successfully in one study.

It is social, breeding in small loose colonies, and shyer and less boisterous than the house sparrow, often holding its tail up. Outside the breeding season it can travel considerable distances, and some breeding areas are vacated entirely in winter.

It nests in holes and crevices in buildings, banks, cliffs and nest boxes. The breeding season runs from April to August, with one or two broods of typically five or six eggs. Both sexes incubate for 12–13 days, and the chicks fledge after about 15–17.5 days. Breeding typically starts at one year.

Breeding success is linked to the invertebrate prey fed to the chicks, and in winter birds gather where seed food is available. A typical adult lives about two years, and the oldest ringed bird reached nearly eleven.

The IUCN Red List classes it as Least Concern, but in the UK it is Red-listed. UK numbers fell by an estimated 93% between 1970 and 2008; the breeding population was 245,000 territories in 2016, up 18% since 1995 but far below 1970s levels. In Europe it has declined since 1980.

The edible frog is a green water frog of central and north-eastern Europe. It is not a true species in the usual sense but a fertile hybrid between the pool frog and the marsh frog, which keeps going by mating with one of its parents.

It reaches up to 12 cm but is mostly under 10 cm, females being larger. The back is light to dark green or brownish with dark spots, often with a light green stripe down the middle, and the backs of the thighs are yellowish or orange with dark bars. The skin is usually smooth and the hind legs long and well webbed. Males have grey nuptial pads on the thumbs and white to grey vocal sacs.

It uses many sun-exposed waters with well-overgrown margins and shallows, from woodland ponds to ditches, lakes and rivers, sometimes in brackish water. It ranges across mid and north-eastern Europe as far as Russia. Introduced colonies in southern England probably all came from releases.

In mixed water frog populations studied in Serbia, insects made up about 88% of the prey items found in stomachs, mostly Hymenoptera, beetles, Lepidoptera and flies. Frogs are opportunistic hunters and their diet varies from site to site. It forages on land mainly at night.

It stays mostly in water and basks a lot. It is mainly active by day but also at night during the breeding season, when males call in dense groups, chiefly in the evening, with grunting or rattling notes. It usually hibernates in soil on land, sometimes underwater, and young frogs can travel several kilometres.

Frogs leave hibernation from about mid-March and eggs are laid from April to mid-July, mostly around mid-May. A female lays 3,000 to 8,000 eggs per season. Tadpoles need two to four months to develop, most transforming between mid-August and mid-September, and frogs mature after two to three years.

The edible frog reproduces by hybridogenesis: it passes on one parental genome unchanged and so needs a parent species to mate with. In the common arrangement it mates with the pool frog, in another with the marsh frog. Some populations are made up only of hybrids, with diploid and triploid frogs together.

It is often the most numerous green frog where it occurs. The sources read give no Red List category for this hybrid. In Serbia, mixed populations of the three water frog forms are rare and only found along the Danube.

Grey Partridge
Perdix perdix

The grey partridge is a plump, ground-living gamebird of European farmland. Once very common and widespread, it has suffered serious declines across most of its range and is now a conservation concern in the UK.

An adult weighs about 390 g with a wing length near 16 cm. The plumage is finely barred grey and brown, with an orange face and throat, chestnut bars on the flanks and a chestnut tail. Males are larger and usually show a U-shaped chestnut patch on the belly; females are duller, with a smaller patch or none.

It is a resident, sedentary bird of lowland farmland, most frequent on arable land in the breeding season. It needs open fields for feeding by day and dense cover to hide in and nest. Chicks depend on cover and on invertebrates, even on rough grazing on hill farms in north-east England.

Adults eat mainly seeds, grain, leaves, roots and shoots, with cereals important in the warmer months. Chicks, in contrast, need protein and feed on insects, including sawfly larvae in a north-east England study, and aphids.

A strictly ground-living bird, it spends the non-breeding season in groups called coveys, usually of 6 to 15 birds and sometimes up to 25, often made up of relatives. Members feed and roost together and keep watch for danger. When threatened, the birds run or fly low and fast, and their bodies can look like clods of earth.

In the UK there is typically one brood a year, with a very large clutch of 13–16 eggs, sometimes more than 20. The female alone incubates for 23–25 days. The downy chicks leave the nest at once and can fly short distances at about two weeks old. Breeding typically starts at one year of age.

Birds of prey such as goshawks and sparrowhawks, and ground predators such as foxes, take adults, eggs and chicks, and higher predation lowers nest success and winter survival. The main driver of decline is agricultural intensification, especially the loss of chick food through pesticide and herbicide use. The birds also disperse seeds in their droppings.

The IUCN lists the species as Least Concern worldwide, but it has declined across Europe. In the UK it is Red-listed: the breeding population was about 37,000 territories in 2016 and fell by 93% between 1967 and 2024. It typically lives about three years once adult, and the oldest ringed bird reached over five.

Allied Rock-wallaby
Petrogale assimilis

The allied rock-wallaby is a medium-sized marsupial of north-eastern Queensland, Australia, that lives among rocky outcrops, cliffs and boulder piles. It shelters in rocks by day and comes out at dusk to feed.

Males average about 4.7 kg and females 4.3 kg. The coat is grey on freshly moulted animals and turns paler to darker brown through the year, with lighter, sandy underparts and limbs, dark paws and feet, and a tail darkening to an indistinct brush at the tip. Some animals show a pale cheek stripe and a dark stripe along the head.

It lives in rocky terrain such as cliffs, slopes, outcrops and boulder piles, usually within tropical woodland and open forest, so its distribution is fragmented. It occurs from Townsville south to the lower Burdekin and Bowen rivers, north-west to Croydon and south-west to Hughenden, and on Palm and Magnetic Islands.

It is a generalist herbivore, eating new grass after rain, browse and small herbs, and supplementing this with fruit, seeds, flowers and some animal matter such as insect larvae. Animal Diversity Web describes it more narrowly as a leaf eater.

It often forages at night and is most visible in the evening, when it moves from rock shelters to open feeding areas, and it stays loyal to its rocky shelter area. Stable bonds form between one adult male and one or two females, which share daytime shelters, groom each other and defend their area, though genetic studies show the bonds are not strictly exclusive.

Breeding is continuous, though extended drought can reduce the number of young that survive. Gestation lasts about 29–34 days and a female usually has one young, which stays in the pouch for about six to seven months and is weaned at about 11 months. Females mature at roughly 18–19 months and males at about two years.

Its home range expands in the wet season and shrinks in the late dry season, following food availability. Known predators include feral cats and red foxes, though it is seldom threatened by predation.

The Mammal Diversity Database lists it as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List, and Animal Diversity Web describes populations as fairly stable. Introduced predators, especially during drought, are a possible threat.

Sea Lamprey
Petromyzon marinus

The sea lamprey is a jawless, eel-like fish of the North Atlantic. Adults live at sea as parasites of other fish and return to rivers to spawn once. Landlocked populations exist in some North American lakes, and in the Great Lakes it is a notorious invader.

The body is scaleless and cartilaginous, with no jaws and no paired fins. The mouth is a round suction disc lined with horny teeth, with a rasping tongue inside. There is a single nostril, an eye on each side of the head, seven gill openings and two dorsal fins. Adults are brownish-gray and usually reach 60 cm, rarely up to 120 cm.

It is anadromous: adults live in the sea and return to freshwater to breed. Its range runs from Norway and Iceland south to North Africa in the Northeast Atlantic, and from Labrador to the Gulf coast of Florida in the west. Larvae live in streams with sandy or gravelly bottoms and slow edges.

Larvae filter-feed on diatoms, algae and detritus. Adults are parasites that attach to fishes, and in the sea sometimes to marine mammals, with their suction mouth and feed on blood and body fluids, often without killing the host. Adults stop feeding when they reach sexual maturity and during spawning.

Adults are highly mobile and have no home range or territory. They are solitary or gather in small groups while attached to hosts. During spawning, males use chemical signals, bile-acid pheromones, to attract females.

Adults run up rivers in spring and early summer, at water temperatures of 10–18 °C, to spawn once and die. Males build nests and females lay tens to hundreds of thousands of small eggs, which hatch after about one to two weeks. The larvae burrow in mud for years, typically 3 to 7 or more, then transform and go to sea, where adults spend about two to three years before returning.

As a parasite, the sea lamprey can harm its host fishes, and adults have few natural predators. Introduced to the Great Lakes, it contributed to the collapse of lake trout, whitefish and cisco fisheries. The catch of lake trout in the upper lakes fell from about 15 million pounds a year to about 300,000 pounds by the early 1960s.

In its native range the species is Least Concern on the IUCN Red List (assessed in 2022). In the Great Lakes, where it is invasive, it is the target of control: lampricides applied to larval streams, plus barriers and traps that stop adults from reaching spawning grounds.

The southern common cuscus is a nocturnal, tree-dwelling marsupial of southern New Guinea and Cape York Peninsula in northern Australia, where it is also called the grey cuscus. It was long treated as a form of other common cuscuses and is now recognised as a species of its own.

It is nocturnal, sheltering by day in tree hollows, and is believed to be solitary. In Australia it is scarce: spotlighting typically turns up about one animal every two to five hours. Home range and movements are not documented in the source consulted.
Very little is known. In Australia, both single young and twins have been recorded. Breeding season, gestation and pouch life are not given in the sources consulted.

Pythons are thought to be significant predators of the species. Its role in the forest as an eater of fruit, seeds and leaves, for example in dispersing seeds, has not been studied in the sources read.

Large White
Pieris brassicae

The large white is a big white butterfly of Europe, North Africa and temperate Asia, a strong flier and migrant. Its caterpillars feed in groups on cabbage-family plants, making it a well-known garden and crop pest.

Wingspan is about 58–63 mm in one source and 63–70 mm in another. The wings are white with black forewing tips extending down the edge; females have two black forewing spots and a hindwing spot, which males lack. The underside is creamy white. The caterpillar is yellowish green with black spots, and its eggs are yellow and skittle-shaped.

It breeds mainly in gardens, allotments and farmland where cabbages grow, and adults also visit meadows, heaths, parks and woodland rides. It occurs across Europe, North Africa and temperate Asia as far as the Himalayas, and was accidentally introduced to Chile.

Caterpillars eat mainly cultivated cabbage, Brussels sprouts and oilseed rape, and also nasturtium, wild mignonette and sea-kale. Young caterpillars feed communally, starting with the outer leaves, and the species is a well-known cabbage pest.

The species is a strong flier and strongly migratory: migrants from continental Europe often reach Britain in spring and autumn, adding to the resident population. Fully grown caterpillars wander away from the food plant to pupate, often under windowsills, eaves, fences or tree trunks.

Females lay yellow eggs in batches of typically 20 to 60 under cabbage leaves, hatching in about ten days. In Britain adults emerge from April, with one or sometimes two further broods, and they fly until mid-September. Chrysalises of the last brood overwinter.

Caterpillars accumulate mustard oils from their food plants, which make them unpalatable to most predators and birds. The wasp Apanteles glomeratus parasitises young caterpillars, reportedly killing a large share of them, and Pteromalus puparum attacks freshly formed pupae.

In Great Britain it is rated Least Concern (2022 Red List) and its European status is not threatened. Even so, UK monitoring shows abundance down 32% between 1976 and 2019 and distribution down 18% between 1973 and 2019.

European pine marten
Martes martes
Native across much of Europe and western Eurasia, the European pine marten varies greatly in abundance and local range. It climbs and forages extensively on the forest floor.

Adults have rich brown fur, a yellow to orange bib on the throat and chest, pale-edged ears and a long, bushy tail. The bib’s colour and outline vary among populations and individuals. Males average larger than females; European samples report adult masses of about 0.8–2.4 kilograms for males and 0.6–1.5 kilograms for females, with ranges varying among studies. The beech marten usually has a white bib that forks toward the forelegs and a pale nose; the pine marten usually has a yellowish bib and dark nose.

The species uses coniferous, deciduous and mixed forests; mature stands are valuable where they provide canopy cover and cavities in old trees or standing deadwood. These structures offer cover and secure resting or breeding sites. In an Irish landscape with few tree cavities, monitored martens also denned in caves, rock crevices, stone walls and wood debris, while avoiding most immature plantations.

The pine marten is an opportunistic omnivore: small mammals, birds and eggs, carrion, invertebrates and fruit all feature in its diet. In Northern Ireland, scat analyses found animal foods prominent in spring and summer and berries important in autumn; birds and small mammals became more important when fruit was scarce. In Galloway, no carrion was detected in denning females’ scats; birds, small mammals and anurans were important, unlike some carrion-containing mixed-sex spring diets reported elsewhere in Scotland.

Pine martens are usually solitary outside mating and mostly nocturnal, though activity varies with season. Scent marks, including conspicuously placed scats, signal occupancy along routes; Spanish observations found marking concentrated at exposed sites and crossroads, especially in May and July. British studies found larger home ranges in males than females, with estimates varying among habitats and food conditions.

Mating in July–August is followed by about seven months of delayed implantation. Implantation in late winter is followed by 30–35 days of development; births occur in late March or April. Females usually have one litter of one to five kits each year. Born blind, deaf and toothless, kits open their eyes at 34–38 days, eat solids from 36–45 days and are weaned at about six weeks. Young emerge at 7–8 weeks; dispersal may start at 12–16 weeks, though some overwinter in their natal territory and leave the following spring. Females use protected dens during the early weeks.

After eating fleshy fruits, pine martens can carry seeds away from parent shrubs in their scats. In a temperate-forest experiment, marked seed mimics embedded in fruit were recovered up to 1,233 metres from feeding stations, a study maximum rather than a typical distance. In the Irish midlands, surveys recorded grey-squirrel decline alongside red-squirrel return where martens recovered. Later analyses across Britain and Ireland found regional associations between marten exposure, lower grey-squirrel occupancy and higher red-squirrel occupancy. In an Irish feeder-camera study, red squirrels became more vigilant and fed less after a marten visit; this short-lived response is a possible mechanism, not proof of the population pattern. These patterns do not show that martens eliminate grey squirrels everywhere or always benefit red squirrels.

The IUCN Red List classified the species as Least Concern globally in an assessment dated 3 March 2015 and published in 2016, citing its wide range and large population despite past declines. This global category does not describe every national population: the Mammal Society lists Great Britain as Least Concern, while martens remain scarce in parts of England and Wales amid habitat fragmentation and persecution. Across Great Britain, the amended Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 protects the species, with schedule coverage varying by jurisdiction. Ireland separately lists the pine marten under its Wildlife Act 1976.

Platypus
Ornithorhynchus anatinus

The platypus is a semi-aquatic Australian mammal and a monotreme: a mammal that lays eggs. Its streamlined, furred body, broad tail and sensitive bill suit a life of searching freshwater beds for food and resting in bank burrows. Females produce milk for their young despite having no nipples. The species occurs naturally in eastern Australia, including Tasmania, in varied freshwater habitats.

Adults have dense waterproof fur, usually dark brown above and lighter below, a flattened bill and a broad tail. The tail stores fat and helps steer. Webbed forefeet provide propulsion; their webs fold back around the claws on land. Hind feet are less webbed and help steer underwater. Males have a sharp hind-ankle spur connected to a venom gland; females lack this functional apparatus. Southern animals tend to be larger than northern ones.

The species ranges through eastern Australia, from tropical Queensland to Tasmania and the Australian Alps. It uses rivers, streams, lakes and farm dams, but needs freshwater for feeding and earthen banks for burrows. Root-stabilised banks offer resting and nesting sites; shaded pools, riffles and gravel or cobble beds support aquatic invertebrates. Platypuses sometimes cross land between water bodies, making catchment connectivity relevant to habitat use.

It hunts small animals, especially bottom-dwelling insect larvae, worms, crustaceans and molluscs. Underwater it closes its eyes, ears and nostrils, locating prey with bill receptors that detect water movement and weak electrical fields from prey muscles. Sweeping its head from side to side helps it orient in murky water. It stores small prey in cheek pouches and grinds food at the surface with horny pads rather than teeth.

Adults are mostly solitary and generally occupy separate resting burrows, although several may use one stretch of water. Activity often peaks from dusk through the night. Forelimbs power swimming, while hind limbs and tail steer; on land, the splayed limbs make walking less efficient. Repeated dives separated by brief surface pauses allow long foraging periods. Grooming maintains the insulating coat needed during extended time in water.

Breeding is seasonal and earlier in northern populations. The female lays one to three soft-shelled eggs in a long bank burrow, which she plugs with soil. Embryos develop partly before laying; external incubation lasts about a week to ten days. Hatchlings are tiny and dependent. The mother secretes milk onto abdominal skin, and young lap it from her fur because she has no nipples. They feed on milk in the burrow and commonly emerge after three to four months, with timing varying by region.

As predators of bottom-dwelling invertebrates, platypuses are part of stream food webs. An Australian field experiment found that their feeding affected invertebrate communities differently in flowing streams and still-water habitats, so ecosystem effects depend on setting. Their reliance on aquatic prey ties them to productive waterways, while bank burrows depend on stable margins. Movement overland may connect catchments, although barriers and dry periods can interrupt dispersal.

A 2022 Australian government report cites the IUCN global category as Near Threatened; this reports a dated assessment record, not a new population estimate. The same report said the platypus was not then listed as nationally threatened under federal or New South Wales law, while relaying a 2020 UNSW review that recommended Vulnerable status. It names threats including bank clearing, altered flows, pollution, fishing by-catch, disease, drought, fire and floods. Victoria listed the species as Vulnerable in 2021. These categories refer to different dates and geographic scales.

European Plaice
Pleuronectes platessa

The European plaice is a right-eyed flatfish of the continental shelf of north-western Europe, found from Iceland and the White Sea southward along the European coast. It is one of the best-studied fish of the North Sea and has been fished there for centuries.

The upper side is brown or greenish-brown with irregular bright red or orange spots, and the underside is white. The skin is smooth with small scales, and a bony ridge runs behind the eyes. Common length is about 40 cm, and the largest fish reach about 100 cm and 7 kg.

It lives on sandy and muddy bottoms from the shore down to about 200 m, usually at 10–50 m, in water of 2–15 °C. Juveniles stay in shallow coastal water and outer estuaries and move deeper as they grow; in the North Sea the Wadden Sea is the most important nursery.

Adults feed mainly on thin-shelled molluscs and polychaete worms, taking bivalves, the siphons of buried clams and, locally, small crustaceans and brittle stars. Adults do not feed during the spawning period.

It rests on the seabed partly buried in sediment. Tagging showed that individuals return to the same spawning and feeding areas, and adults travel between them by using tidal streams: they drift in midwater with the current and stay on the bottom when it turns.

Spawning takes place offshore in restricted areas, peaking in early January in the eastern Channel and mid-February in the German Bight. A 35 cm female may produce 60,000–100,000 pelagic eggs of 1.7–2.2 mm. The eggs and larvae drift for three to four months; the fish settles on the bottom only after metamorphosis, when the left eye has moved to the right side. In the North Sea, males mature at two to three years and females at four to five.

Plaice larvae eat small planktonic animals such as appendicularians and copepods, while older fish feed on the seabed. The eggs are eaten by other fish: many were found in herring and sprat stomachs, so egg survival varies with their abundance.

The IUCN lists the species as Least Concern (assessed 2022, as reported by FishBase). It is an important commercial species, taken mostly by beam trawls in a mixed fishery with sole. In the North Sea, landings rose from about 70,000 t in the late 1950s to about 170,000 t in the late 1980s, then fell below 60,000 t by 2005, and earlier maturation has been linked to fishing pressure.

Polar bear
Ursus maritimus

The polar bear is a marine mammal whose life follows Arctic sea ice, the platform from which it reaches seals. Its fur, fat, smell, and broad paws suit cold water and ice, but it hunts most effectively from sea ice. Seasonal ice loss changes both access to food and the distances bears must travel.

Adult males commonly weigh about 270–545 kg and measure roughly 2.4–3 m from nose to tail; adult females are smaller, commonly about 180–320 kg. These are broad wild adult ranges: age, region, season, and fat reserves change an individual’s mass. The long neck and narrow head help distinguish the species, while the coat’s translucent hairs scatter visible light so the dense fur appears cream or white. Beneath the fur lie dark skin and a thick layer of subcutaneous fat; the hairs do not channel sunlight to the skin like fibre-optic cables. Dense underfur and guard hairs trap still air, while blubber adds insulation in water. Broad paws spread weight on weak ice and paddle during swimming; partial webbing increases paddle efficiency. Small, round ears and a short tail reduce exposed surfaces. A keen sense of smell helps locate seals, while the muzzle and claws help seize prey.

Its range circles the Arctic, from Alaska and Canada to Greenland, Svalbard, and Russia; movements vary with coastlines and ice. Productive sea ice over continental shelves gives bears access to seals resting or raising pups. Some follow seasonal ice toward shore at breakup, while others remain farther north; an ashore summer is not universal. Many land maternity dens are excavated in snow, but in Western and Southern Hudson Bay some females begin in frozen peat or earth before extending the den into accumulating snow. In some other regions, pregnant bears also den on stable sea ice.

Ringed seals are staple prey; bearded seals also matter, depending on local availability. A bear may wait by a breathing hole, detect a seal by smell, and seize it as it surfaces, or stalk one resting on ice. Bears often eat blubber and skin first, leaving remains for foxes, ravens, gulls, and other bears. They digest and store these lipids efficiently as fat, which fuels movement, warmth, reproduction, and fasting. On land they may eat birds, eggs, plants, fish, carrion, or refuse; most terrestrial foods are scattered or relatively low in energy and generally cannot replace seal hunting. Rich marine-mammal carcasses, such as whale or walrus remains, can nevertheless be locally important. Bears can enter a facultative fasting state even while actively searching for food: stored lipids supply energy while protein is spared. The duration and energetic cost of fasting vary among bears.

Adults are usually solitary outside mating and family groups; females use large home ranges whose size varies with local land and sea ice. Regional movements may follow freeze-up and breakup, while elsewhere bears remain on ice in summer. In spring, males follow tracks and scent trails left by females’ feet. Experiments show that bears can distinguish scent donors by sex and reproductive condition, so trails carry more than a simple signal of presence. When seals are unavailable, some rest while others search for land foods; either strategy spends stored energy and can still bring weight loss.

Mating occurs on sea ice in spring. After fertilization, the embryo pauses and usually implants in autumn only if the female has built adequate reserves; this is delayed implantation. The interval from mating to birth is about 195–265 days, but active fetal development lasts only two to three months. Only pregnant females enter maternity dens, often in October or November, and births occur from November to early January depending on latitude. The mother fasts while giving birth and nursing; this winter dormancy is not species-wide hibernation. Litters contain one to three cubs, usually twins; newborns are blind and weigh about 0.5 kg. They grow quickly on fat-rich milk and stay with their mother for about 2.5–3 years, learning to hunt and swim.

As the Arctic’s largest terrestrial predator, the polar bear links sea ice to marine food webs: ice algae support small consumers, then fish and seals, which feed bears. Seal remains feed Arctic foxes, gulls, and ravens, extending each kill’s benefit to other species. Seasonal fat storage links prey abundance with survival and cub production, carrying effects of ice change through the ecosystem.

The IUCN Polar Bear Specialist Group’s global assessment, published in 2015, classified the polar bear as Vulnerable. It identified climate-driven sea-ice loss as the leading long-term threat because ice provides access to seals. Longer open-water seasons can force some bears ashore, lengthen fasting, and affect condition, reproduction, or survival; effects differ by region and period. In Canada, COSEWIC assessed the species as Special Concern in 2018; individual management-unit trends are separate from the global Red List and may be uncertain or dated. In 1973, the five range states signed an agreement for coordinated protection and management of feeding, denning, and migration habitat.

Powderblue surgeonfish
Acanthurus leucosternon

The powderblue surgeonfish is a reef-dwelling member of the surgeonfish family, Acanthuridae, native to the tropical Indian Ocean. Its blue body, dark head and white chest make it distinctive. It grazes on algae growing on reefs and may feed alone or join other fish. The species is best known from shallow reefs, where feeding grounds and territorial behaviour are tied to patches of algal growth.

Its deep body is flattened from side to side. A broad white band crosses the chest from the pectoral-fin bases, and a narrow pale line outlines the lower face. The dorsal fin is yellow with a pale edge and dark submarginal line; the tail base and paired spines are yellow. A pale crescent marks the dark tail fin. Each side of the tail base bears a sharp spine that folds into a groove and can be raised when the fish bends its tail. The Andaman Sea account reports specimens up to 23 cm. FishBase lists a maximum total length of 54 cm.

It ranges through the tropical Indian Ocean, from eastern Africa to the Andaman Sea and Indonesia, reaching Bali; records include Cocos (Keeling) and Christmas islands. It occupies shallow coastal and island reefs, especially reef flats and upper outer slopes, generally down to about 25 metres. These sunlit surfaces support the benthic algae it eats, although feeding grounds vary among reef zones.

Adults are herbivores that crop benthic algae, including short microalgal turf on hard reef surfaces. At Aldabra, researchers observed adults defending permanent feeding territories containing these algal mats. FishBase also records feeding on scattered algae and small growths in crevices. Each jaw bears a row of incisor-like teeth. High-speed recordings show the fish grasping algae, then pulling them free by rotating its head and closed jaws downward. An articulation within the lower jaw enables this movement without turning the whole body sideways. This may help feeding in strong currents, although that ecological advantage remains an interpretation of the mechanics.

Individuals forage alone or gather in feeding groups. At Aldabra, adults defended permanent algal territories against other fishes, protecting access to food. The study describes territorial defence within and between species among surgeonfishes.

The sexes are separate, and observations describe paired spawning during the breeding period. FishBase describes the species as monogamous. At Aldabra, the study documented pairs among permanently territorial surgeonfishes and no parental care in its study group. Eggs and sperm are released into open water for external fertilization. Surgeonfish yolk-sac larvae float near the surface, then swim and feed after the yolk is absorbed. They pass through a pelagic acronurus stage before reef settlement.

By cropping attached algae, this fish uses food produced on reef surfaces and participates in grazing those patches. Herbivorous reef fishes can limit algae that impede coral recruitment, although the strength of this effect varies among species. At Aldabra, adults defended small turf plots against competitors, dividing access to algal resources. Territories focus grazing on defended patches. Feeding aggregations bring several fish to shared food areas.

The IUCN Red List account lists the species as Least Concern, assessed on 3 May 2010 and published in 2012. On the Kenyan coast, people harvest it for subsistence and commercial fisheries. This species is also collected for the aquarium trade. Dunnock
Prunella modularis
The dunnock is a small, unobtrusive brown-and-grey bird that creeps about under hedges and shrubs. Behind its modest looks lies one of the most complicated mating systems found among birds.

About 13–14.5 cm long, roughly the size of a house sparrow, and weighing about 21 g. The back is brown streaked with black, the head and breast are grey, the legs pinkish and the bill is thin and pointed, unlike a sparrow’s. The sexes look alike; juveniles are browner and less grey.

It lives in much of Europe and south-west Asia. In Britain it is most frequent in villages, and is also common in gardens, scrub, farmland, woodland and towns, wherever dense low vegetation gives cover.
It feeds mainly on spiders and insects, which it finds by hopping on the ground, and eats seeds as well. It sometimes visits feeders but more often picks up spilt food beneath them.

Shy and secretive, it creeps through undergrowth in a mouse-like way, often flicking its wings. Males sing a loud, squeaky warble from high perches, mostly from March to May, and rival males flick their wings and call loudly.

Both males and females may mate with several partners, so a female can be helped by two males to raise her chicks. The cup nest is built low in dense shrubs and holds typically 4–5 unspotted blue eggs, incubated by the female for 14–15 days. Chicks fledge after 12–14.5 days. Breeding typically starts at one year.

A ground-feeding insect and seed eater, the dunnock depends on dense low cover. Natural food, especially seed, runs short in late winter, and from mid-February dunnocks on farmland turn to feeding stations.

The IUCN Red List classes the species as Least Concern. In the UK it is Amber-listed: about 2.5 million territories were estimated in 2016, and numbers fell by 43% between 1967 and 2024, with the sharpest drop from the mid-1970s to the mid-1980s and a partial recovery since. The oldest ringed bird lived over 10 years.

Madagascar Flying Fox
Pteropus rufus

The Madagascar flying fox is the largest bat of Madagascar and is found nowhere else. It is a fruit bat that roosts in groups in trees and is listed as Vulnerable, mainly because of hunting and the loss of its forest.

A large bat with a body about 24–25 cm long, a wingspan of roughly 1.2 m and a mass of 500–750 g, males being heavier than females. It has a long pointed muzzle, pointed ears, large eyes and no obvious tail. The upper body is yellowish brown, the underside dark brown, the face and throat seal-brown and the neck yellowish to reddish brown.

It lives only in Madagascar. It is described as roosting mainly in humid coastal forest on sandy soil, from sea level to about 800 m. In the Mangoro valley, in the centre-east, roosts were in small, isolated fragments of degraded humid forest of 2.2–28.7 ha and in two Eucalyptus plantations, all outside protected areas.

It mostly chews fruit to drink the juice and spits out the dry pulp and seeds. It also eats pollen and leaves, and sometimes insects. In the Mangoro valley, droppings contained remains of native forest trees, cultivated fruits and Eucalyptus flowers, so it can feed in landscapes changed by people.

It roosts in groups of hundreds to thousands, often at the same site all year, but is very sensitive to disturbance and may move away. Numbers at a roost vary a lot from month to month: in the Mangoro valley only two of six sites held bats at every visit. In the mating season, dominant males defend territories on the roost trees. It relies mainly on scent and sound rather than echolocation.

Mating takes place in April–May, with males gripping the female’s scruff. Gestation is given as 100–150 days, and delayed implantation is possible. Usually a single pup is born, around October, and is nursed for four to five months. Both sexes mature at 1.5 to 2 years. Three Mangoro roosts were occupied only from September to March, possibly as nursery roosts.

It is an important seed disperser for many plants of the coastal forests, and the only fruit-eater there able to carry seeds over long distances, which may help link forest fragments. Pollen found on its body suggests it also pollinates some plants. Young that fall from the roost are taken by the Madagascar harrier-hawk.

It is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List. Hunting for bushmeat was found at three of the Mangoro roosts, and fire and forest clearance are widespread; the authors of that study noted that no conservation plan existed for the species. Hunting also targets roosts and feeding trees elsewhere, and only some roosts are formally protected.

Seychelles Fruit Bat
Pteropus seychellensis

The Seychelles fruit bat, called sousouri locally, is the largest bat of the Seychelles and one of the archipelago’s two native mammals. It is a flying fox that feeds on fruit and flowers and is found across the central granitic islands.

A large fruit bat with dark brown fur, black wings and a bright orange-yellow head and neck, and a prominent snout. It weighs up to about 600 g, with a wingspan of up to 1.2 m according to one source and up to 1.5 m according to another.

It occurs widely on the central granitic islands of the Seychelles, such as Mahé, Praslin and Cousine, and roosts in treetops. It can fly between neighbouring islands, for example between Praslin and Cousin. The Mammal Diversity Database now restricts the species to the Seychelles, treating the Comoros population as a separate species.

It eats fruit, nectar and pollen, including cultivated mangoes and papayas, and relies on a keen sense of smell and good eyesight to find food. It feeds noisily in fruiting trees, sometimes all night.

Colonies roost together in treetops during the heat of the day, hanging by one foot, and the bats fly out in the late afternoon to feed. They are most often seen at dusk and dawn, and in greater numbers from November to February, when food is more plentiful, according to a Cousine Island account. On very calm days a few skim the sea and dip their chests in the water, for reasons not fully understood.

The sources consulted give no breeding season, litter size or age at maturity. The Seychelles Ministry of Environment announced a study to document the species’ feeding and breeding patterns, which suggests these remain poorly documented.
As a pollinator and seed disperser, it helps native plants regenerate and is an important part of island ecosystems. A Seychelles environmentalist has noted that it disperses seeds of endemic plants.

The Mammal Diversity Database lists it as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List. A 2004 report estimated about 8,500 bats in the Seychelles, and no newer count had been made by the time of a recent news article. It is hunted for a curry considered a delicacy, though no law forbids this, and it also suffers collisions with infrastructure and has been linked to power outages on Mahé.

Puma
Puma concolor

The puma, also called cougar or mountain lion, is a large cat native to the Americas. Usually solitary, it ranges from western Canada through much of South America. Its presence across varied landscapes makes it one of the continent’s most widely distributed native mammals.

Adults have a tawny, grey-brown or reddish coat, usually paler underneath, with a small head, rounded ears, powerful hindquarters and a long, thick tail. Adults lack spots; kittens are spotted, and their markings fade as they grow.

Pumas occupy forests, scrub, grasslands, deserts and wetlands, from lowlands to mountains. They use places with prey and cover, including dense vegetation, rocky crevices and caves. Habitat use varies locally: Florida panthers, for example, use swamp forest and wooded hammocks.

This carnivore takes locally available prey. Deer are important across much of North America; elk, moose, wild pigs, guanacos, hares and smaller mammals may also be eaten. Pumas stalk and ambush prey, then cover large carcasses to return for later meals.

Adults generally live alone, except during mating and while females raise young. Home ranges can overlap; a male’s range may encompass several females. Scent marks, scraped ground and scratched logs signal occupancy. Pumas may be active by day or night, often around dusk and dawn.

Pumas breed year-round, though some populations have seasonal peaks. After about three months, a female gives birth to one to six kittens in a den. Spotted at birth, they eat meat at six weeks and stay with her for about a year.

As a large predator, the puma hunts herbivores and can affect where prey feed and move. Its effects depend on local conditions and interactions with other predators. Yellowstone research examines cougars alongside wolves, bears and elk; carcasses also provide food for scavengers.

The IUCN assessment published in 2015 classified the species as Least Concern, while noting uncertainty and suspected declines in parts of Central and South America. Habitat loss, fragmentation, persecution, hunting and depleted prey threaten some populations. Connected habitat and reduced conflict are conservation priorities.

European rabbit
Oryctolagus cuniculus

The European rabbit is a burrowing lagomorph native to the Iberian Peninsula and parts of southwestern Europe. Human transport and escape from domestication have spread it far beyond that range, so the same species can be a threatened native animal in one landscape and an invasive grazer in another. It is also the wild ancestor of domestic rabbits.

A wild adult is usually 38–50 cm long and weighs 1.5–2.5 kg. Its compact body, short ears and strong hind legs support quick dashes between feeding ground and cover. The grey-brown coat is paler underneath; the white underside of its short tail flashes as it bounds away. Compared with a hare, it has shorter ears and legs and relies on underground refuge. Its young are helpless at birth, unlike furred, mobile leverets.

In its native range the rabbit favours open, short-grass ground near dense cover, especially where soft soil allows digging. Scrub, grassland, woodland edges and some farms or urban spaces provide food and shelter, though ploughing can destroy burrows. A warren’s linked entrances and chambers offer escape routes and protected places to rest or nest. Where soil is unsuitable, rabbits use surface cover such as dense vegetation.

The rabbit selectively eats grasses, tender shoots, leaves and buds, sometimes roots or bark. Because plant fibre is difficult to digest, microbes ferment fine particles in its enlarged caecum while coarse particles pass quickly through the gut. The rabbit periodically re-ingests soft, nutrient-rich caecotrophs, allowing their contents another passage through the small intestine. These differ from ordinary firm, dry pellets, which carry much of the indigestible fibre and are not recycled.

European rabbits are unusually social for a leporid. Where food and soil permit, groups share warrens and defend a territory. Several females and males may live together; dominance shapes access to space and mates, with conflict clearest between males. Rabbits feed mainly at dusk and night, then retreat underground by day. Scent marks signal occupancy, while a hind-foot thump warns nearby animals of danger. Group boundaries and a familiar warren provide security.

Wild breeding is seasonal and responds to food and local conditions. After mating-triggered ovulation, gestation lasts about 30 days and litters commonly contain five or six young. A doe digs a nursery burrow and lines its nest with dry plants and fur. Kittens are born naked and blind, unlike furred, open-eyed hare leverets. The mother returns briefly to nurse, then leaves the nest concealed. Young leave the nest and are weaned at about four weeks; first-year mortality can be high from predation, weather and disease.

In Mediterranean Iberia, rabbits are key prey for many predators, including the Iberian lynx and Spanish imperial eagle. Their grazing changes plant cover, while burrows shelter other animals and communal latrines concentrate nutrients that affect plant growth. Rabbits therefore act as ecosystem engineers, with effects that depend on density and habitat. Their role in native food webs can become damaging when dense introduced populations overgraze and compete with local wildlife.

The latest global IUCN assessment located was published in 2019 from an assessment dated 15 August 2018. It classified rabbits as Endangered across their native range in Spain, Portugal and southern France. Myxomatosis, rabbit haemorrhagic disease and habitat degradation drove declines; GI.2/RHDV2 added pressure after reaching Iberia in 2011–12. A 2025 study of hunting records from about 6,000 central-Spain estates found declines in most areas without emergency crop-damage control during 2009–22, but trends differed where rabbits damage crops. In Australia, feral rabbits are widespread and harm native vegetation and threatened species. Conservation priorities therefore differ between the native range and introduced populations.

Common raccoon dog
Nyctereutes procyonoides

The common raccoon dog is a stocky member of the dog family, native to mainland East Asia. Its adaptable habits let it use woodland, wetlands, open country and some human-modified landscapes. Its dark facial mask gives the head a raccoon-like appearance, but its build and ancestry are canid. The species has also established far beyond its original Asian range after people released it for fur production in Europe.

Despite its name and dark eye mask, it is a canid, not a raccoon. Adults average about 56 cm in head-and-body length and roughly 4.5 kg, with local seasonal variation. A broad head, short legs and dense, shaggy coat give the animal a low, rounded outline; the dark mask contrasts with paler cheek fur. The tail is short and bushy, about 18 cm in one specialist account, and lacks the bold rings of a true raccoon. Winter fur grows longer and thicker, while moulting restores a shorter coat for warmer months. These dimensions describe wild adult reference samples, not a maximum: body mass changes substantially before and during winter rest.

In its native range it occurs from China and Mongolia through Korea and the Russian Far East to northern Vietnam. Woodland edges, river valleys, scrub and wet ground offer cover beside varied feeding sites. Breeding adults use a den to raise their young.

This opportunistic omnivore shifts between plant foods and animal prey as local supplies change, and it also scavenges carrion. Estonian stomach samples illustrate the seasonal shift: autumn diets contained more amphibians and invertebrates, while winter samples held more small mammals, carrion and human-associated foods. Cereals and fruits at supplementary feeding sites, especially those for wild boar, supplied plant foods in that study.

Raccoon dogs often form a breeding pair whose members use overlapping ranges and cooperate around the den. Field tracking in Germany found males guarding nursing pups while females made longer foraging trips. They are mainly active at night and around twilight, although local conditions and human disturbance can alter when they move. In southern Finland, tracked animals usually stayed in dens during midwinter but sometimes wandered even in the coldest months. In cold northern winters, individuals can enter long but intermittent bouts of reduced activity, rather than one uniform, deep hibernation.

In southern Finland, mating peaks in March; gestation lasts about 60–62 days, births are concentrated in May, and the mean litter at birth is about nine. Litter size and the proportion of females breeding vary with age, food and local conditions. Pups remain in a den for about six weeks, then begin travelling with their parents. Juveniles in Finland usually begin dispersing in August, with most leaving the natal range by September or October.

In northern European wetlands, its predation can affect frogs and nesting waterbirds, although broad population effects remain difficult to establish. Local studies have found amphibians and bird eggs among its foods, so vulnerable island or shoreline breeding sites may face concentrated pressure. It also scavenges carcasses and competes with other medium-sized carnivores for this winter resource, though studies reviewed in Europe found little evidence of severe competition with foxes or badgers. In its introduced range, it can carry parasites and pathogens, making disease transmission an ecological and veterinary concern alongside predation.

The global IUCN assessment, last assessed on 1 March 2016 and published in 2016, classified the raccoon dog taxon then recognized as Nyctereutes procyonoides as Least Concern with a stable trend; at that time it included Japanese populations now recognized separately by the Mammal Diversity Database. This historic category is not a new assessment of the current mainland species. Fur-farming releases in the former Soviet Union began a European expansion that continues to shape management. Between 1929 and 1955, about 9,100 animals were released in European Russia, and descendants spread into northern, eastern and central Europe. Its listing as an invasive alien species of Union concern applies from 2 February 2019. The current Union-list framework requires prevention or management measures. The main concerns are predation at sensitive local breeding sites and the spread of parasites and disease; evidence for continent-wide declines in native birds remains limited.

Keel-billed toucan
Ramphastos sulfuratus

The keel-billed toucan is a resident canopy bird of humid forests, ranging from southern Mexico through Central America to northwestern South America. Its large, multicoloured bill gives it the alternate name rainbow-billed toucan. In a pasture-dominated landscape in Mexico, tracked birds selected forest remnants while also using several wooded and agricultural habitats.

Adults are about 50 cm long. The body is black with a yellow throat and chest, white rump, red undertail feathers, blue eye skin and blue feet. The sexes look alike, though males may be slightly larger. The oversized green bill has orange, red and blue accents and can approach a third of body length. A species sheet describes a lightweight honeycomb-like core under a keratin covering; direct mechanical tests used the related toco toucan. Two toes point forward and two back to grip branches.

The species occupies humid tropical forest, mainly in the middle and upper canopy. It also visits edges, secondary growth and trees retained in pasture or cropland. In Los Tuxtlas, Mexico, six birds followed for 349 hours preferred forest remnants at both landscape and local scales. Their activities were similar among habitat types, suggesting some altered patches still supplied resources. This regional result does not mean open land replaces intact forest across the range.

Fruit is the staple, including figs and palm fruits. A toucan can pluck fruit from branches too slender to support its body, swallow it whole, then regurgitate or pass seeds away from the parent tree. It also eats insects and small vertebrates; eggs and nestlings are recorded prey. One published observation documents a keel-billed toucan taking vertebrate carrion, an unusual opportunistic food rather than evidence of a regular habit.

Keel-billed toucans move between fruiting trees, often in small flocks; older accounts report groups of six to twelve. They hop along branches and fly between trees with rapid wingbeats followed by a glide. In one Mexican study, foraging and perching each occupied about 35–40% of observed time, while calling and social interactions each took 10% or less. They also roost in tree cavities; group composition and year-round social bonds remain poorly documented.

The toucan nests in a natural tree hollow or an old cavity made by another bird. Species accounts report two to four eggs, incubated by both parents, who also feed the helpless chicks. They hatch after about 16–20 days and remain in the cavity while growing; fledging is reported around eight to nine weeks. These timings come from limited, partly older natural-history sources and may vary locally.

Fruit feeding carries seeds between feeding and resting sites. A Panamanian study of Virola surinamensis found heavier weevil attack beneath and near parent trees; dispersal beyond 20 metres by large birds, including keel-billed toucans, appeared more favorable for seedling survival. Gut passage has different effects in different plants. In an experiment with captive keel-billed toucans, Ficus insipida seeds recovered from droppings did not germinate significantly better than uneaten controls. Seed transport and enhanced germination are therefore distinct processes.

BirdLife International’s global IUCN assessment, dated 18 March 2021, lists the species as Near Threatened with a decreasing trend. It estimates 50,000–499,999 mature birds and links decline to habitat loss, degradation, hunting and trapping. Earlier assessments through 2016 listed Least Concern; that category is no longer current.

Common raven
Corvus corax

The Common Raven is a large member of the crow family, occupying much of the Northern Hemisphere. Its success comes from a flexible way of life: it can hunt, scavenge, eat plant matter, and exploit food made available by people.

An adult measures about 58–69 cm from bill to tail, with a wingspan of roughly 120–150 cm and a mass of about 0.7–1.6 kg; body dimensions vary geographically. It is entirely black, with a heavy bill, thick neck, shaggy throat feathers, and a long, wedge-shaped tail. In comparison, a Carrion Crow is smaller and has a squarer tail, a slimmer bill, and a less shaggy throat; size and silhouette together are more useful than colour, which is black in both. Young ravens look browner and duller than adults. The raven\'s broad, pointed wings support slow flaps, soaring, and agile rolls or steep dives. Its deep, rough croak carries far, and the species also makes a varied set of softer calls; vocal sounds serve contact, alarm, and territorial contexts.

Across its range, the raven uses tundra, mountains, coasts, forests, open country, farmland, and some settlements. It needs suitable ledges, trees, or structures for nesting and enough food nearby; consequently, local abundance depends on landscape and resources rather than a single preferred habitat.

The raven is an opportunistic omnivore. It takes carrion, small mammals, birds and their eggs or nestlings, fish, insects and other invertebrates, as well as grains, fruit, buds, and human food waste. Small prey may be swallowed whole, while hairs, feathers, bones, and other poorly digested remains can be brought back up in compact pellets. It hides surplus food in caches, particularly when a large carcass or other temporary bounty is available, and may move or conceal a cache when competitors are nearby.

Breeding adults usually live as territorial pairs and may remain paired year-round; they defend the nest area and key food patches. Outside these territories, young birds and nonbreeders often gather, and several ravens may converge on a carcass, rubbish tip, or seabird colony. Its characteristic call is a harsh, resonant croak; during courtship, ravens perform tumbling aerial displays. In captive studies, ravens have adjusted cache placement after observing competitors. In one controlled experiment, they guarded caches in response to a rival’s sounds when a peephole allowed that bird to see the caching area; this suggests sensitivity to visual access, without establishing human-like thought.

A pair generally establishes and defends a territory before nesting. It builds a bulky stick platform in a tree, on a cliff, or on a human-made structure, then lines the cup with softer material. The female usually incubates a clutch of three to seven eggs for about 20–25 days, while the male often brings food. Chicks hatch helpless, with closed eyes and sparse down; both parents feed them. They leave the nest after roughly four to seven weeks, though fledging does not mean immediate independence. Ravens commonly raise one brood in a year, and young birds may not breed until two to four years old.

At carcasses, ravens feed alongside other scavengers; in some seabird colonies, groups take eggs and chicks, so their effects on prey are strongly local. The species is thus both a consumer of carrion and a predator whose impact can matter for vulnerable nesting birds.

The 2021 European Red List assessment classified the breeding population as Least Concern and increasing; this regional assessment is not a guarantee that every local population is secure. In Britain, raven numbers fell historically and the range contracted westward; as persecution eased from the mid-twentieth century, populations recovered and expanded again. The return has renewed conflicts with livestock interests and conservation managers where ravens take vulnerable young or eggs. The British Trust for Ornithology reports licensed control in Scotland and concern that illegal killing may still affect some local populations.

Red-backed Shrike
Lanius collurio

The red-backed shrike is a small songbird that hunts like a bird of prey from perches and impales its catches on thorns. It breeds across much of Europe and migrates to southern Africa, but has almost vanished as a breeding bird in Britain.

A little larger but slimmer than a house sparrow, an adult weighs about 28 g with a wing near 95 mm. The male has a bluish-grey head, a black mask, a bright chestnut back and a thick black bill. Shrikes typically perch in the open.

It favours semi-open landscapes with hedges and thorny bushes beside insect-rich grassland, ideally sunny places with short or bare ground where prey can be reached. In Sweden, territories were small, about 0.5–1 hectare, with plenty of well-spread perches.

Its prey is mostly small and medium-sized insects, which are also what the chicks are fed, together with some small vertebrates. Shrikes take their catches to a larder, where they impale them on a thorn or wedge them into branches to store them for later.

Shrikes watch for prey from the tops of bushes, fence posts and wires. The red-backed shrike is a long-distance migrant: late-spring arrivals may wait for food to become available in the African wet season before crossing the Sahara. In Britain it is now a scarce passage visitor, mostly in May–June and August–October.

A clutch is typically four to six eggs, incubated by the female for about 14 days. The chicks hatch naked and fledge at 14–15 days. There is usually one brood a season, occasionally two. Nests are placed low in thorny shrubs; in a Turkish study blackberry was the most common nest site.

The shrike depends on thorny cover and insect-rich open ground close together. Nest predation was the main cause of nest failure in a study in northern Turkey. Intensive farming that removes insect-rich grassland next to hedges is expected to cause long-term declines.

The IUCN lists the species as Least Concern worldwide. In the UK it is Red-listed and legally protected, with about three breeding pairs in 2013–17 after it became effectively extinct as a breeder in 1989. Its British breeding range contracted by 88% between 1968–72 and 2008–11.

Red deer
Cervus elaphus

The red deer is a large hoofed ruminant native to Europe, the Atlas Mountains, Anatolia, the Caucasus and northwestern Iran. Current classifications distinguish it from the wapiti and Central Asian red deer. Introduced populations occur elsewhere, including New Zealand.

Adults have a reddish-brown summer coat, greyer or darker in winter; it is not spotted. Stags are generally larger and darker than hinds and have a pale rump. Males grow branching antlers, shed annually and regrow them beneath velvet, which they rub off when growth ends. Point count does not reliably show age.

It uses deciduous and coniferous woods, edges, scrub, grasslands and moorland, feeding in open areas with cover nearby. Habitat use varies regionally. Introduced deer released in New Zealand since 1851 now occupy forest and tussock country on the main islands.

This flexible herbivore grazes grasses and herbs and browses leaves, shoots and shrubs. Spring growth, winter bark and ferns, and other foods vary with season and location. As a ruminant, it regurgitates and rechews plant matter; diets differ between woodland and open habitats.

Hinds often associate with calves and younger deer; mature stags tend to keep apart outside breeding season. In autumn, males roar, scent-mark and display. Rivals may walk parallel, then clash with locked antlers; successful stags gather temporary harems. The sexes usually separate again after the rut.

In Europe, the rut usually occurs in autumn, though timing varies with latitude and hemisphere. After about eight months, a hind generally bears one calf in late spring or early summer. Its reddish coat has pale spots that fade within months. At first it hides in vegetation while its mother feeds nearby.

Grazing and browsing change vegetation, depending on deer density and habitat. In Swiss subalpine grasslands, seeds in red deer dung showed that deer disperse plants between feeding and resting areas. This can shape local plant communities, though effects vary by site.

The global IUCN assessment, last assessed on 12 October 2015 and published in 2018, classified red deer as Least Concern because of its wide range and presumed large populations. This dated assessment is not a new count; it also noted regional contractions and likely declines. In introduced New Zealand populations, deer can damage native plants and forest regeneration, prompting control. Taxonomic limits in Asia have changed since that assessment.

Red fox
Vulpes vulpes

The red fox is an adaptable canid native across much of the Northern Hemisphere, from Arctic regions to North Africa, Central America and Asia. It occupies wild, farmed and urban landscapes, while local abundance and habits depend on food, cover and human pressures.

Its familiar coat is rusty red above, pale underneath, with dark lower legs and a bushy tail often tipped white. Colour is variable: individuals may be pale, dark or cross-patterned. The pointed muzzle, upright ears and slender build remain useful features across these forms.

Red foxes use forests, scrub, grasslands, deserts, mountains, farmland and city edges; they often benefit from a patchwork of cover and open feeding ground. In Australia they were introduced for hunting in the nineteenth century and spread widely, though distribution remains uneven.

It is an opportunistic feeder, taking small mammals such as rodents and rabbits when available, as well as birds, invertebrates, reptiles, fruit and carrion. Proportions shift with season and place. Urban foxes may use discarded food, while Australian foxes consume introduced and native prey.

Foxes often forage alone around dusk or at night, but schedules vary with disturbance and food. They cache surplus food in small buried stores. A pair may share a territory; some populations form family groups where related nonbreeders help provision or guard young.

Breeding is seasonal, with timing shifting across the species’ range. After about seven to eight weeks of pregnancy, a vixen gives birth in a den. Cubs are born blind, leave after several weeks and are gradually weaned; litter size and helper care vary among populations.

As predator and scavenger, the fox consumes many kinds of animal matter and sometimes fruit, but its effects depend on local food webs. In Australia, government reviews link introduced fox predation to declines in several native ground-dwelling mammals and birds; other pressures can also contribute.

The global IUCN assessment published in 2021 retained Least Concern, based on the assessment dated 2016 and the species’ broad range. This category does not describe every local population. In Australia, introduced foxes are managed as invasive predators because of risks to native wildlife.

Red junglefowl
Gallus gallus

The red junglefowl is a wild galliform bird of the pheasant family, native to South and Southeast Asia and the principal wild ancestor of the domestic chicken. Whole-genome comparisons support an early contribution from the Southeast Asian subspecies Gallus gallus spadiceus, followed by gene flow among chicken populations and other junglefowl; domestication was not a simple, isolated event. Some regional chicken genomes also carry introgressed DNA from grey junglefowl (Gallus sonneratii), with lesser or rarer signals from Ceylon junglefowl (Gallus lafayettii) and green junglefowl (Gallus varius); these findings do not displace red junglefowl as the main ancestor.

The wild adult male has a bright red comb and wattles, orange-gold neck feathers, a dark iridescent body, and long curved feathers over the tail; total length can reach about 70 centimetres including that tail. Females are smaller-looking and mottled brown, with a short tail and camouflage suited to nesting on the ground. A study of the Thai subspecies Gallus gallus spadiceus found breeding males with long golden neck hackles, unlike the shorter black feathers outside the breeding period. A wild-type outline alone cannot establish genetic purity, because domestic ancestry may be invisible in appearance. Domestic chickens have also been selected for rapid growth, so breed size and body form are not reliable norms for wild birds.

Its native range spans the Indian subcontinent and much of mainland and island Southeast Asia, with regional subspecies occupying different areas. It uses old and secondary forest, mangroves, and forest edges, often feeding in a clearing or plantation beside cover.

This opportunistic omnivore takes seeds, fruits, and small invertebrates, including ants, beetles, and termites; the mix changes with local and seasonal availability. It scratches through soil and leaf litter with its feet before pecking at food, often visiting open ground in the early morning and evening. Its digestive tract includes a crop and muscular gizzard; the gizzard mechanically breaks down ingested food.

Wary and mostly terrestrial, red junglefowl can fly strongly when alarmed and commonly roost in trees at night. Field observations describe small, changing groups: a male may accompany one or several females, while solitary males and females are also seen. Males crow repeatedly, often before dawn, and crowing helps reveal their presence; calls and displays also communicate between birds, though social patterns vary with place and season.

Breeding schedules differ by region: a two-year study of the subspecies Gallus gallus spadiceus in Malaysian agricultural landscapes recorded nests year-round, with a local peak in December. Nests averaged about four eggs, and captive incubation lasted roughly 19.5 days, close to three weeks. In Hainan, field researchers observed only females tending the brood, while accounts from southern Yunnan report both sexes incubating eggs; parental roles vary among the populations studied. Chicks hatch covered in down and leave the nest soon; a natural-history account places full feathering at about four to five weeks and sexual maturity near five months, somewhat later in females.

Field observations and local reports from Thailand and Malaysia identify wild cats and birds of prey among predators of adult junglefowl. In Hainan, nest monitoring found predation to be a major cause of breeding failure, with coucals and rodents recorded at experimental nests and reptiles proposed as other potential predators.

BirdLife International’s global IUCN assessment published in 2024 classifies the species as Least Concern, a global risk category that does not guarantee the security of each local population. An Indian Wildlife Institute of India project reported a fragmented distribution and growing pressures in several states, and found ten domestic-chicken hybrids among 220 birds sampled at captive centres. A 2023 genome comparison found domestic ancestry of about 20–50 percent in the modern wild populations sampled, relative to museum birds collected roughly a century earlier, with strong variation among individuals and places; habitat change and contact with free-ranging poultry remain local concerns.
