Red kangaroo
Osphranter rufus

The red kangaroo is a large grazing marsupial of mainland Australia’s arid and semi-arid interior. It uses open plains, grasslands and shrublands. Its fortunes follow irregular rain: fresh growth can support breeding and population increases, while prolonged drought reduces forage and may lower numbers.

The largest living marsupial, it shows striking sexual dimorphism. Males may reach 1.4 m head-and-body length and 92 kg; females about 1.1 m and 39 kg. Males are often rusty red and females blue-grey, though shades vary. Both have pale undersides and black-and-white cheek markings, including a light stripe from mouth towards ear. Fast travel uses powerful hindlimb bounds; a long muscular tail swings with the legs and helps reduce trunk pitch. During each bound, ankle extensor tendons stretch under load and recoil, returning stored elastic energy. This reduces the muscle work needed to repeat the movement; oxygen use on level ground changes little across hopping speeds, though uphill travel costs more.

Across mainland Australia’s dry interior, it inhabits open plains, grassland, shrubland and savanna woodland. Scattered trees and shrubs offer shade from intense heat. In hot conditions, blood flow rises in superficial vessels of the forelegs; licking spreads moisture there, which evaporates and carries heat away. Radio-tracking in Western Australia found adult females’ core ranges stable and compact, with grazing and shelter together; males used larger areas. Drought increased adult dispersal, and journeys to water were prominent. Local distribution thus reflects vegetation and changing forage as well as water access.

It mainly grazes grasses. A 12-year study in southern Australian arid shrubland found more forbs in wet seasons and more shrub browsing in dry conditions; grasses still formed almost 90% of sampled food in severe drought. Microbes ferment fibrous plants in its enlarged forestomach, making nutrients available. Experiments with red kangaroos found methane yield varied with food intake. Green herbage supplies some water, but drought reduces both forage and moisture.

Groups are small and temporary rather than fixed family units: one field study in northwestern New South Wales recorded a mean of 2.2 animals, with size and membership changing frequently. Radio-tracking found adult females relatively sedentary with stable ranges, while subadult males dispersed widely; drought increased adult movements. Male ranges were larger and could include the core areas of several females. In an arid-pasture study, grazing peaked between dusk and dawn, when animals spent over 60% of their time grazing.

Breeding can occur year-round, with more births in spring and summer, and responds to food and rainfall. After about 33 days, one very underdeveloped young crawls into the pouch and attaches to a teat. A female may mate again soon after birth. If the pouch young still suckles, the new embryo can pause at the blastocyst stage; this embryonic diapause delays development until the older joey permanently leaves the pouch. The joey exits permanently at about eight months but may continue suckling for months.

The red kangaroo is prey for predators such as dingoes and shares arid rangelands with livestock. In a long-term southern Australian study, dietary overlap with sheep increased in drought, when both relied heavily on grasses; potential competition grew as pasture deteriorated. An analysis of 1978–2002 aerial counts across four South Australian areas modelled population growth against rainfall, harvest, kangaroo density and domestic herbivore density. The best model found a positive statistical association with livestock density, which the authors proposed could reflect resource availability beyond rainfall. These findings describe regional pastoral systems, not a universal effect of livestock.

The Mammal Diversity Database reported the IUCN global category as Least Concern when consulted in October 2026, reflecting the species’ broad Australian range and large population. This status coexists with marked local fluctuations: drought can reduce forage and survival, while favourable rain can support population growth. Management figures are regional. A New South Wales government report dated 17 December 2025 set commercial quotas for 2026 and gave 2025 estimates for monitored zones; these guide harvest in that state rather than estimate the global population.

Red Knot
Calidris canutus
The red knot is a stocky Arctic-breeding wader that winters in huge, swirling flocks on estuaries. It is a long-distance migrant, and in Britain it depends on a small number of large estuaries.

In Britain an adult weighs about 138 g, with a wing near 169 mm, roughly Blackbird-sized and larger than a Dunlin. The bill is straight and about as long as the head, and the legs have a greenish tint. In winter it is pale grey above and white below; in spring and summer the face, chest and belly turn brick-red. Young birds look scalloped.

In winter and on migration it feeds on muddy and sandy shores, especially large estuaries, and it is generally absent from rocky coasts. It breeds on high, barren Arctic tundra, usually near a pond or stream.

Away from the breeding grounds the red knot eats small invertebrates from intertidal mud, mainly small molluscs, with some marine worms and crustaceans. On the Arctic tundra it feeds mostly on insects, especially flies, and early in the season on plant material.

Outside the breeding season knots gather in large flocks that flash their pale underwings as they twist and turn. They breed in the Arctic and migrate south in autumn, with a pronounced passage through the UK. Some birds from the Canadian Arctic apparently cross the Greenland ice cap to winter in Britain and Europe.

A pair typically raises one brood a year, laying four eggs (sometimes three) in a shallow ground scrape lined with leaves, lichen and moss. Both sexes incubate for 21–22 days, and the chicks fledge after about 18–20 days. Breeding usually starts at two years of age.

Knots rely on a few rich estuaries as feeding grounds both on migration and in winter, so changes there matter greatly. Threats named include barrages, sea-level rise and human disturbance of feeding areas; in North America, the loss of horseshoe crab eggs at Delaware Bay has hit the species hard.

The IUCN Red List classes the species as Near Threatened, and it is Amber-listed in the UK. About 265,000 knots winter in the UK (2012–17); BTO reports a 15% rise between 1998 and 2023, while the RSPB describes an earlier 13% fall over 25 years. The oldest ringed bird lived over 27 years.

Red squirrel
Sciurus vulgaris

The Eurasian red squirrel is a small tree-dwelling rodent widespread across Europe and northern Asia. Curved claws and powerful hind limbs aid climbing and leaping; its long bushy tail helps balance and thermoregulation. It feeds mainly on plant foods that change with forest and season. Usually foraging alone, individuals may share winter nests. Autumn scatter-hoarding stores food and sometimes disperses seeds. The species remains widespread globally, despite sharp regional declines in parts of Britain and Italy.

This slender squirrel has prominent eyes, a long bushy tail and, in winter, often tufted ears. Its coat ranges from bright red or chestnut to brown, greyish or nearly black, commonly with a pale underside; the name does not describe every animal. In a Hokkaido subspecies, specimens had lighter winter coats and more pronounced seasonal colour shifts, but appearance also varies geographically. The North American eastern grey squirrel, Sciurus carolinensis, is a different species; colour alone cannot distinguish them because red squirrels may also be grey or dark.

Red squirrels inhabit boreal conifer forests, mixed and broad-leaved woods, wooded parks and some fragmented landscapes. Local food and tree structure shape their use of habitat: conifer seeds may be dependable, while deciduous woods supply seasonal nuts, buds and fruit. In one northern Greek mixed forest, four adults used the canopy extensively, especially small branches and terminal twigs. This study illustrates how connected crowns provide feeding and escape routes, not a universal habitat preference. Squirrels build twig nests high in trees and line them with softer material; they may also use cavities.

Seeds and nuts are staple foods, but the menu shifts with season and habitat. Cones and seeds may dominate in conifer forest; buds, shoots and flowers become important at other times, supplemented by berries, fungi and deciduous seeds. Incisors strip cone scales and open hard seed coverings. Some animal matter is also eaten, though plants predominate. Rather than one larder, squirrels bury food in many separate caches. In a Japanese Korean-pine forest, researchers documented red squirrels carrying cones and burying seed clusters; those observations describe that population and tree system.

Curved claws grip bark, letting squirrels climb trunks and move onto slender branches. In northern Greece, clawed climbing aided vertical travel and retreat to trees after ground feeding; quadrupedal movement and sitting helped squirrels use terminal twigs and handle food. Jumps cross gaps between crowns. The long tail helps balance and thermoregulation, while hind limbs support climbing and leaps. Red squirrels forage mostly alone rather than in stable troops. Their home ranges overlap, and familiar individuals may tolerate one another or share nests during cold periods. Space use shifts with food and breeding conditions.

Breeding timing varies with latitude, food and condition. Gestation lasts about 38–39 days. When a female is receptive, several males may follow and compete; mating does not establish a lasting pair bond, and males provide no routine care. The female raises the litter in a nest and may move young if disturbed. Newborns are blind and sparsely furred; eyes open at about a month, and young begin leaving the nest at roughly 40–45 days. They sample solid food before weaning at around 8–10 weeks, remaining under maternal care during early life. Litter size and breeding frequency vary, so regional averages are not fixed outputs for the species.

Scatter-hoarding links squirrel feeding with forest regeneration. In Hokkaido, Japan, red squirrels carried Korean-pine cones from source trees and buried seeds in small clusters. One study found seedlings as far as 600 m from parent trees; another recorded them up to 1.8 km from the nearest source. These are separate site-specific observations, not a typical distance. Squirrels recover some caches; seeds left in suitable microsites may germinate. This interaction is documented for Korean pine in parts of East Asia, not every tree or squirrel population. Caches also provide food when fresh resources are scarce.

The 2023 IUCN global assessment classifies the species as Least Concern because of its broad Eurasian range; this does not mean all populations are secure. In Britain, introduced eastern grey squirrels compete with red squirrels and can carry squirrelpox virus, which causes severe disease and mortality in reds. English surveillance from 1993–2005 found cases in areas where seropositive greys also occurred, supporting a reservoir link in that setting. Grey squirrels and squirrelpox are not a universal Eurasian threat. Habitat fragmentation, forestry and other local pressures also matter, so conservation needs depend on region.

This large colubrid snake ranges across Southeast Asia, from the Andaman Islands to the Philippines and Indonesian archipelagos. Records include Myanmar, Thailand, Vietnam, Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia and the Philippines. Its common name reflects the frequent green body and rusty-red tail, though brown and other colour forms occur.

Adults generally measure 1.6–2.3 metres. Singapore’s National Parks Board lists the species at 2.4 metres. The body is laterally compressed, with broad smooth belly scales for gripping branches, a dark eye stripe and often green colouring with a rusty tail.
It inhabits tropical forests, including mangroves, lowland woods and forest edges, and may also occur in plantations or gardens. Fully arboreal, it moves through the branches above the ground.
Its prey includes birds and eggs, lizards, bats and small mammals. It hunts in trees, sometimes hanging from a branch to seize prey moving through the canopy, including bats in flight.
Diurnal and arboreal, it moves through branches above the ground. When threatened, it can inflate its body and strike defensively.

Mating occurs in trees, and the female lays eggs in a sheltered place. In one captive case, a fertile clutch of four eggs was incubated at 30°C; hatchlings emerged over days 87–89. The three young first shed 10–14 days after hatching, then accepted pinkie mice; all fed regularly within a month. The same report noted a second fertile clutch after the female had been kept apart from a male, suggesting stored sperm.
As a tree-dwelling predator, it feeds on animals that use the canopy, including birds, bats and lizards, as well as small mammals.

The IUCN assessment published in 2012 classified the species as Least Concern. Singapore’s National Parks Board records it in Bukit Timah and Central Catchment forest reserves, a local occurrence within its much wider range.

Goldcrest
Regulus regulus

The goldcrest is one of Europe’s smallest birds, a restless, tiny insect-eater of conifer woods. Its numbers swing with the severity of winter, and large clutches help it recover from the heavy losses cold weather causes.

It weighs only 5–6 g and is about 9 cm long. The body is dull greyish-green with a pale belly, a large dark eye in a pale eye ring, two white wing bars and a thin bill. A yellow crown stripe bordered with black is orange in the male and yellow in the female; juveniles lack the stripe.

In the breeding season it is most frequent in coniferous woodland, and it also uses mixed woods, parks and gardens with mature trees, mostly staying in the treetops. In winter it moves lower, into hedges and scrub.
It is mainly insectivorous, picking small invertebrates such as insects and spiders from foliage, especially conifer needles, and often hanging upside down while it hunts.

It is very active and restless, and its high-pitched, repetitive song is the best way to find it. In winter it often joins roaming flocks of tits. Autumn brings arrivals from Scandinavia and Russia, which boost winter numbers in Britain.

In Britain the first clutch is laid around early May and there are typically two broods. A clutch is typically six to eight eggs and can reach twelve. The female alone incubates for about 16–19 days, and the downy chicks fledge after roughly 16.5–18 days. Breeding usually begins at one year.

Cold winters are the main check on its numbers: RSPB reports that about eight in ten goldcrests die each winter. Predators include the Eurasian sparrowhawk and the pygmy owl. A typical bird lives about two years, and the oldest ringed one in Britain reached just over five.

The IUCN Red List classes it as Least Concern, and it is Green-listed in the UK. The UK breeding population was estimated at 790,000 territories in 2016, though it fluctuates with winter weather, and numbers in Europe have declined since 1980.

Rhinopithecus avunculus

The Tonkin snub-nosed monkey is a leaf-eating monkey found only in northern Vietnam, and the only snub-nosed monkey of subtropical forests. It is Critically Endangered and has long been counted among the 25 most endangered primates in the world.

A fairly slender monkey with a body of 51–65 cm and a tail of 66–92 cm, longer than the body. Males average about 13.8 kg and females about 8.3 kg. The back, outer limbs, hands and feet are black, while the chest, elbows and inner limbs are creamy white. The nose is upturned and the skin around it and the eyes is bare and pale blue; the throat is orange, more strongly in males. Juveniles are greyish black.

It lives in subtropical broad-leaf and bamboo evergreen forest with monsoon rains, usually on limestone hills below 1,000 m. It is confined to northern Vietnam and now survives in a few areas of karst limestone peaks, among them the Khau Ca conservation area.

It eats mainly leaves, especially bamboo and other evergreen leaves, but is not strictly a leaf-eater: fruit, flowers and seeds are also eaten. One study listed 31 food species from 21 plant families. Like other leaf-eating monkeys it has a stomach with several compartments and strong jaw muscles for tough plant food.

It is active by day and lives in the trees, walking on all fours and also climbing and leaping. Groups are either all-male or made of one male with several females and young. Groups split and merge and the species does not appear to be territorial. It sleeps on lower branches near steep slopes, sheltered from cold night winds, and its main call is a hiccup-like sound used as alarm and contact.

The mating system is polygynous. Gestation lasts about 200 days and females give birth to one or two young in spring or summer. Females mature at about 4 years and males at about 7. The breeding season, the interval between births and the length of nursing have not been reported.

As a plant-eater it may shape the vegetation around it, and the fruit it eats may help spread seeds. Humans are its only confirmed predator; snakes, large birds of prey and forest cats probably take some, but this has not been confirmed.

It is considered Critically Endangered and is listed in CITES Appendix I. A 2025 census by Fauna & Flora counted about 160 animals in the Khau Ca conservation area, a stable population, and the total is estimated at about 250. Hunting for food and traditional medicine was once the key threat and is illegal; the main current threats are habitat loss and deforestation, notably for farmland, along with bamboo harvesting and gold mining.

The bearded pygmy chameleon is a tiny, short-tailed chameleon of the forests of eastern Tanzania and south-eastern Kenya. It lives close to the ground, among leaf litter and low bushes. Its scientific name means short-tailed.

A very small chameleon, about 8 cm long, named for its scaly throat with two chin lobes. It can change colour among brown, yellow, green, orange and black, to show stress or attract a mate. Sleeping in the open, it can flatten its body and show a side stripe that looks like a dead leaf.

It lives in lowland forest of eastern Tanzania and south-eastern Kenya, including submontane and coastal forest, on the leafy forest floor and in low bushes. The Rondo Plateau in Tanzania is one confirmed locality, and the type locality is Derema in the Usambara Mountains.
It eats small insects, which it hunts in the leaf litter of the forest floor and in low shrubs.
It is usually active during the day and clings to the twigs and leaves of low bushes, hunting close to the ground. Beyond this, little about its daily life is documented in the sources consulted.
The Reptile Database lists the species as egg-laying. Clutch size, incubation time and age at maturity are not given in the sources consulted, so they are left out here.
Its dead-leaf look helps it escape the notice of predators, and it depends on the rich leafy understorey of healthy evergreen forest, where it hunts small insects.

It is classed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List according to a conservation charity and the Reptile Database. Habitat loss and deforestation are the main threats: its estimated range covers about 163,800 square kilometres, but forest makes up less than a tenth of that area.

Rissa tridactyla

The black-legged kittiwake is a medium-sized, strictly maritime gull that spends most of its life at sea and comes ashore to nest in noisy cliff colonies. It is Britain’s most numerous gull, but its numbers have fallen steeply.

An adult is 38–40 cm long with a white head and body, a mid-grey back and wings, a dark eye, a small yellow bill and long black legs. The wing tips are solid black, as if dipped in ink, with no white spots. Adults weigh about 310–434 g, and young birds take three years to reach full adult plumage.

It breeds mainly on rocky sea cliffs, also on buildings and bridges: more than 1,000 pairs nest on window ledges and bridges along the River Tyne. In Britain the main strongholds are in Scotland, notably Orkney and Shetland, and densities are highest on the east coast from Flamborough Head to Orkney.
It feeds mainly on sandeels and other shoaling fish caught at sea. Unlike related gulls, it does not scavenge from chip shops. It is a surface feeder that takes small fish and invertebrates.

After breeding it moves out onto the high seas of the Atlantic for the winter and is rarely seen from land. It flies with tern-like wingbeats and can land on narrow ledges in strong wind. At the nest it faces the cliff, so that its tail projects over the edge.

A pair raises one brood a year. The typical clutch is two eggs (one to three), incubated by both sexes for about 25–32 days. The downy chicks are semi-precocial and fledge after roughly 33–54 days. Breeding typically starts at age four. Males tend to reuse the same nest site each year.

Breeding success in Britain is probably linked to sandeel numbers, which are affected by fisheries and by sea surface temperatures. Kittiwakes often depend on one main food source, so a shortage of that prey can hit them hard. Their colonies are often shared with guillemots and razorbills.

The BTO lists the species as Vulnerable globally on the IUCN Red List and Red-listed in the UK. The UK breeding population was 205,000 pairs in 2015, and the British breeding population has nearly halved since the 1970s. A bird that reaches breeding age lives about 12 years; the oldest ringed bird reached over 28.

The European robin is a small, upright songbird of Europe, western Asia and parts of North Africa, where its range spans woodland, scrub and settled landscapes. It is the robin of European gardens, a member of the Old World flycatcher family, Muscicapidae. The similarly orange-breasted American robin is a different species, Turdus migratorius, in the thrush family; the shared English name reflects appearance, not close relationship. Many robins stay near their breeding range, while birds from colder northern and eastern populations move south or west for winter.

Adults of both sexes look alike: a bright orange-red face and breast form a bib against a grey-blue border, brown upperparts and a pale belly. At about 14 centimetres long, adults weigh roughly 14–25 grams across published reference ranges; it has a short, fine bill and long legs for its upright, quick-hopping gait. Newly fledged birds lack orange and are mottled brown with golden spots, a less conspicuous pattern that blends into leaf litter. In a partial post-juvenile moult during summer, some feathers are replaced and orange-red feathers begin to appear on the breast. The sexes remain difficult to tell apart by sight.

Robins use cool, shaded places with low cover, such as deciduous woods, hedges, scrub, parks and gardens. Dense vegetation gives shelter and song perches, while patches of open soil or leaf litter make small prey accessible. Nests occupy sheltered sites, from natural cover to unusual human-made places such as flower pots. Their comfort around people is especially familiar in Britain and Ireland; elsewhere in Europe they can be more wary, so garden behaviour is not universal.

Most of the year, robins hunt small invertebrates such as insects and earthworms at ground level. From a low perch, one may drop onto visible prey and return to cover, or hop across litter and seize prey after a brief pause. In autumn and winter, berries and other fruits can also supplement animal food; the balance varies by season and region.

Outside breeding season, a robin is usually solitary and defends feeding space from others. Both sexes can hold territories and sing during winter, when the song is often more plaintive and drawn out than the breeding song. This year-round defence helps secure familiar cover and safe feeding patches as well as food. The species is partly migratory: some populations are resident, some move only in part, and northern or eastern breeders travel to western Europe and North Africa. In Britain, local birds are joined by winter visitors from farther north and east; migration varies among populations.

The female builds a cup of moss, leaves and grass, lined with hair or plant fibres, in a cavity or other sheltered site. In Britain, four or five eggs are typical; she incubates them for about 14–16 days. The chicks are altricial, meaning they hatch helpless and need parental warmth and food. Both parents feed chicks until they fledge at about two weeks; the male may keep feeding them when the female starts a second brood. A pair often raises a second brood when conditions permit.

By taking insects and other invertebrates, robins are small predators in leaf litter and low vegetation; adults can in turn be hunted by birds of prey. A Lithuanian nest-box study recorded pine martens and dormice as nest predators; other observations describe cuckoo chicks ejecting host eggs or young. In southern France, a winter study documented seasonal fruit eating and inferred that robins may contribute to seed dispersal in Mediterranean scrub. When gardeners dig, robins seize worms and grubs exposed in the soil.

BirdLife International’s 2018 global assessment classified the European robin as Least Concern, reflecting its very large range and population. Global security does not mean every local population is stable. In the UK, Birds of Conservation Concern 5 (2021) places the robin on the Green List. Monitoring shows a long-term increase, interrupted by falls after severe winters and local declines in earlier atlas comparisons. Cold spells can reduce survival by making food harder to find.

Rock pigeon
Columba livia

The Rock Pigeon is a dove that nests on natural cliffs and city ledges. Its close association with people began through domestication thousands of years ago; the familiar urban bird is usually descended from domestic pigeons that escaped or were released. This history has carried feral populations around the world, while genuinely wild populations retain a much narrower native range. The distinction matters because plentiful city flocks do not by themselves show that wild cliff populations are secure.

A typical wild adult is blue-grey, with two black bars across each wing, a white patch on the lower back, and a dark band near the tail tip. Green and purplish iridescence flashes on the neck as the bird turns in the light. Adults usually measure 30–36 cm, weigh 265–380 g and span 50–67 cm; sex and population cause variation. Domestication has produced many colours and patterns, and feral birds may show them too, so a grey, barred individual is not automatically a wild Rock Pigeon.

The wild native range extends across parts of Europe, North Africa, the Middle East, Central Asia and South Asia, but millennia of domestic movement blur its limits and make some remnant wild populations hard to distinguish from feral birds. Rock Pigeons nest in cliff crevices, usually near open ground where seeds are accessible. Farms provide grain and water, while cliffs offer protected roosts and nest sites. In towns, roofs, bridges and ledges provide similar shelter, explaining urban success without making cities the species’ original home.

The bill picks up seeds and grains from the ground, along with small fruits, green plant material and occasional invertebrates. A pigeon can drink by immersing its bill and drawing water continuously, an unusual ability among birds that avoids repeated head tipping. Swallowed food may pause in the crop, an expandable part of the oesophagus that stores and moistens it. In the glandular stomach (proventriculus), hydrochloric acid activates pepsin for chemical digestion; the muscular gizzard grinds seeds, often aided by swallowed grit, before the small intestine completes digestion and absorbs nutrients. Urban scraps broaden the menu but do not erase the species’ seed-eating biology.

Outside the breeding season, pigeons often gather to feed and roost. Males bow and coo during courtship, and may regurgitate food to a partner. Experiments on trained homing pigeons show a sun compass corrected by the internal clock and olfactory map cues for locating home after unfamiliar releases; the strength of odor-based navigation varies among regions. GPS-tracked pigeons also follow learned visual routes over familiar terrain. When the sun compass is unavailable, tests support a magnetic compass; these experiments study domestic birds released away from their loft.

Pairs may keep the same partner through successive nesting attempts, but long-term bonds can break when breeding conditions change. The male brings twigs while the female arranges them into a loose platform on a ledge or in a cavity. A clutch is usually two white eggs; both adults share incubation for about 18 days, with the male commonly taking the middle of the day. Hatchlings are helpless, sparsely downy nestlings that remain in the nest. Both parents feed crop milk: prolactin stimulates crop-lining cells to multiply and shed, producing a secretion rich in protein and fat but poor in carbohydrates, not milk from mammary glands. Parents gradually add softened or regurgitated seeds as chicks grow. Young usually leave the nest at 25–32 days and continue to be fed as they learn to forage.

By eating seeds on open ground, Rock Pigeons link wild plants and cultivated grain to the animals that prey on birds. They are themselves taken by predators including Peregrine Falcons; in cities, these raptors sometimes nest on tall buildings and hunt pigeons among the rooftops. Nesting colonies leave conspicuous droppings on building ledges. Their broad diet also lets them exploit food discarded or provided by people, tying local flocks to human activity.

The IUCN lists the Rock Pigeon globally as Least Concern. The cited assessment is the 2016 version amended in 2019. That broad category can obscure a problem for wild birds: domestic and feral pigeons interbreed with cliff-dwelling Rock Pigeons, introducing genes and sometimes replacing local ancestry. Research in Britain and Ireland found the least introgression in the Outer Hebrides and varying admixture elsewhere; plumage alone cannot reliably identify an individual’s ancestry. The 2021 European Red List assessment classed the species as Least Concern but its regional population trend was unknown. Cornell’s North American summary reported a 46% decline from 1966 to 2015, a regional signal rather than a global estimate.

Rook
Corvus frugilegus

The rook is a social Eurasian crow of open farmland, ranging from western Europe across northern Asia to eastern Siberia. Most western populations stay near their breeding grounds, while birds farther north and east move south for winter.

Adults measure about 44–46 cm long, with a wingspan of 81–99 cm; their black plumage often shines blue or violet in sunlight. Bare pale skin around the slim bill distinguishes adults from carrion crows; juveniles retain facial feathers until roughly six months old.

Rooks are most common in rural fields and villages, nesting in mature trees between farmland; they also enter towns when suitable habitat is available. They use parks and churchyards where large trees provide nesting sites.

As an omnivore, the rook eats earthworms and insect larvae, while grain and other plant foods also make up a major part of its diet. In spring it may pull up germinating crops, and occasionally eats small vertebrates, eggs or carrion.

Rooks feed in noisy flocks and gather at dusk before flying to communal night roosts, sometimes alongside jackdaws. Their varied calls signal recognition between mates or aggression, while long-term pair bonds persist within the colony.

Established pairs build or repair a cup of twigs high in a tree, often reusing a site in a rookery that may persist for years. The female usually incubates three or four eggs for about 15–16 days while the male brings food; after hatching, both parents feed the helpless chicks. Young leave the nest at about 32–34 days but remain dependent on parental feeding for some time before becoming independent.

By eating soil invertebrates, rooks remove some crop pests, yet their taste for newly sown grain and emerging seedlings can bring them into conflict with farmers. Their feeding therefore links the seasonal supply of field prey and seeds with both agricultural benefits and losses.

Its global conservation status is Least Concern, although local fortunes differ. In Britain, breeding numbers have declined since around 2000, while the causes remain unclear. Across its range, changing farmland, pesticide-treated seed and persecution are documented pressures.

Desert rosy boa
Lichanura trivirgata
The desert rosy boa, Lichanura trivirgata, is a small boa native to the southwestern United States and northwestern Mexico.

Females are generally larger than males. Arizona individuals reach 95 centimetres; three dark lengthwise bands and vertical oval pupils are characteristic. The head is small and the tail relatively blunt. A stout body usually has a pale grey background with brown or orange bands.

Its range covers western Arizona, Sonora and most of Baja California; California records are limited to far southern San Diego County. It shelters in rocky desert foothills, scrub and canyon crevices, and may use burrows where surface cover is scarce. Coastal California populations formerly grouped with this boa are now treated as Lichanura orcutti.
Small mammals and birds are its main prey. It subdues them by constriction, wrapping its body around the animal.

Usually solitary, it moves slowly and stays sheltered under rocks, in crevices or inside burrows. In Arizona it is mostly nocturnal or crepuscular, yet may move on spring mornings and on mild or overcast days.

During spring courtship, a male follows the female’s scent, tongue-flicks over her body and strokes her flanks with pelvic spurs before mating. After several months of internal development, females bear live young that soon become independent. In Arizona, births occur in late summer or early autumn, with three to fourteen young recorded per litter.
It hunts rodents in rocky desert habitats, acting as a ground-level predator in arid food webs.
Wild collection for pets occurred historically, while captive breeding later met much of the demand. An IUCN assessment published in 2007 classified the species as Least Concern.

Ruddy Turnstone
Arenaria interpres

The ruddy turnstone is a stocky, colourful shorebird that takes its name from its habit of flipping over stones and seaweed to find food. It breeds in the Arctic and winters on coasts across much of the world.

A small, robust wader, smaller than a Redshank, weighing roughly 95–125 g with a wing of about 157 mm. It has chestnut and black upperparts, a black-and-white head, white underparts, orange legs and a short, slightly upturned black bill. The sexes look alike.
It breeds on Arctic tundra and does not nest in Britain. In winter it uses almost any coastal habitat, with a preference for rocky shores, but also sandy beaches and estuaries.

It flips small stones on the tideline to find small crustaceans and insects, and is famously indiscriminate about what it eats. It also takes molluscs, worms and carrion, and can open barnacles and bivalves with its stout bill.

Turnstones spend much of their time creeping and fluttering over rocks, turning things over as they go. Outside the breeding season they form flocks, often mixed with other shorebirds. Summering birds in Britain are usually young individuals that have not reached breeding condition.

A pair typically raises one brood a year, laying four eggs (sometimes three to five). The female mainly incubates them for 22–24 days. The precocial chicks fledge after about 19–21 days. Breeding typically starts at two years of age.

On the breeding grounds, jaegers, gulls, ravens and foxes take mostly eggs and young; adults are rarely caught, mainly by falcons and owls. The turnstone in turn preys on large numbers of insects on the tundra and of crustaceans and molluscs on the shore.

The IUCN Red List classes the species as Least Concern, but it is Amber-listed in the UK. About 43,000 turnstones winter in the UK (2012–17); numbers fell by 17% between 1998 and 2023, but the long decline since the mid-1980s has levelled off. Threats include coastal habitat change and disturbance. The oldest ringed bird reached 20 years.
